tldr: By designing uniform RGB illumination that thoroughly eliminates ghost lights and glare, the authors developed a markerless visuo-tactile sensor and demonstrated that a TimeSformer can detect fine-grained 8-directional slip on unseen objects with 91.5% accuracy.
hero_caption: Configuration of the proposed visuo-tactile sensor and grasping experiments. (a) Sensor structure including the detachable contact part, (b) Data collection setup mounted on a robot hand for slip experiments, and (c) Clear tactile images obtained when pressed against 15 daily objects.
overview:
For robots to manipulate objects as dexterously as humans, tactile feedback is essential to instantly detect minute slips at the contact interface and regrasp with appropriate force. Recently, visuo-tactile sensors (VTS) that capture the deformation of flexible rubber using a miniature camera have become dominant. However, most conventional sensors rely on tracking grid-like markers embedded inside the rubber. This obscures the fine surface texture, and slip detection has mostly remained a simple binary classification of whether slip occurred or not.

To address this, the authors proposed an approach that directly captures fine texture changes across the contact surface without using markers. For the hardware, they optimized internal illumination placement and diffusion plates, adopting an optical design that completely directs reflection ghost light from the acrylic support plate outside the camera's field of view and focus depth. This achieves sub-millimeter (error around 72 µm) 3D depth reconstruction alongside crisp texture capture under glare-free, extremely uniform RGB illumination.

Furthermore, they built a large-scale tactile dataset using 15 objects (about 8,000 slip sequences and about 19,000 static images) and developed a dual-head model based on the spatiotemporal transformer "TimeSformer". This model simultaneously predicts the contact state (static, pressing, slip) and an 8-directional vector (in 45-degree intervals) when slip occurs.

Experimental results demonstrated that even on unseen objects never touched during training, the model achieves exceptionally high accuracies of 95.5% for contact states and 91.5% for slip directions. It also reached 98.8% accuracy in object classification from static images, proving the effectiveness of a high-performance tactile foundation model directly relevant to dexterous manipulation.
contributions: Designed a markerless visuo-tactile sensor that directs ghost reflections from the acrylic plate outside the field of view and extracts fine textures via glare-free, uniform RGB illumination.
Constructed a high-quality RGB-D tactile benchmark with synchronized dense 3D depth information for slip sequences (63,400 frames) and static images (approx. 19,000 frames) across 15 objects.

Proposed a Dual-Head TimeSformer that simultaneously predicts contact states (3 classes) and slip directions (8 directions), achieving highly accurate slip detection even on unseen objects via a masked joint loss function.

sections.heading: Why We Need Markerless Visuo-Tactile Sensors Now
sections.summary: While visuo-tactile sensors provide high-resolution tactile information, conventional marker tracking obscures surface texture and limits slip detection to binary classification. This work combines a markerless design using uniform illumination with a spatiotemporal transformer, achieving 8-directional slip estimation via fine texture tracking and highly accurate object classification.
sections.details:
When robots grasp and manipulate objects, vision alone struggles with occlusion and estimating contact forces, making tactile feedback from fingertips critical. Among tactile approaches, visuo-tactile sensors that track elastic body deformation with internal cameras have advanced rapidly because they offer spatial resolution orders of magnitude higher than traditional electronic skins.

However, existing visuo-tactile sensors have faced two major issues:
- First is the "reliance on physical markers." Many sensors place markers such as black dots on or inside the rubber, calculating shear forces and slip from their displacements. But the markers themselves hide the fine geometry and texture of the contact surface, losing subtle topography information.
- Second is the "coarseness of slip detection." Most datasets and algorithms focus on binary classification of "slipping vs. not slipping," lacking detailed directional information on "which direction it slipped" that robots need to decide how to adjust grasp poses.

To solve both challenges simultaneously, this work developed a markerless structure with uniform internal RGB illumination and 3D shape reconstruction via high-precision photometric stereo (a method estimating surface normals and shapes from varying illumination directions). Furthermore, by adopting TimeSformer, which has succeeded in video recognition, the authors present a framework that robustly estimates 8-directional slip even on unseen objects from spatiotemporal movement patterns of fine textures.

sections.heading: The State of Slip Detection and Material Classification with Deep Learning
sections.summary: Slip detection has evolved from early CNN-LSTMs to ViTs with attention mechanisms, yet many methods remain marker-dependent or limited to coarse classifications. This work adopts TimeSformer to directly capture 8-directional slip from spatiotemporal texture changes without relying on optical flow or marker tracking.
sections.details:
Robotic slip detection was previously tackled using optical flow or CNN-LSTM temporal models. Recently, introducing Vision Transformers (ViTs) and self-attention mechanisms to focus on contact areas and capture dynamic slip phenomena has become popular.

However, most prior works still rely on tracking physical marker displacements, or their classification remains coarse, like "static," "slip," and "press." In advanced manipulation, unless a robot immediately understands which direction an object is escaping from the fingertips, it cannot perform appropriate pushing-back or regrasping control.

This work leverages the Divided Space-Time Attention of the TimeSformer video classification model. Without explicit markers, this enables precise tracking of the spatiotemporal motion of subtle contact textures captured under uniform illumination.

Regarding material and object classification through touch, many conventional large datasets (such as Touch in the Wild) were collected using marker-based sensors or lacked depth information. This work fills this benchmark gap by building a multi-task dataset covering 15 diverse objects with synchronized high-precision depth information for all samples.

sections.heading: Optical Design and Depth Reconstruction that Suppress Glare to Reveal Fine Geometry
sections.summary: The sensor is compact at 37×34×34 mm and features a modular design where the wearable elastomer can be replaced independently. Uniform illumination is achieved via PCB RGB light placement and frosted glass diffusers, while ghost reflections from the acrylic plate are directed away from the camera view and focus, achieving high-accuracy depth reconstruction with an RMSE of 0.072 mm.
sections.details:
The sensor features an extremely compact footprint of 37 mm × 34 mm × 34 mm for easy integration into standard robotic grippers.

### III-A Overall Sensor Design and Optical Engineering
The structure consists of three main modules:
- Contact module: An elastomer made of transparent silicone (Solaris) coated with a white pigment reflective layer.
- Illumination module: A dedicated PCB with RGB LEDs and frosted glass light diffusers.
- Signal acquisition module: A miniature RGB camera positioned at the base.

The key design innovation here is the "elimination of ghost images from the acrylic support plate." Surface reflections from the clear acrylic backing that supports the elastomer normally create ghost images of the light sources in camera frames, severely degrading photometric stereo accuracy. The authors meticulously calculated the distance and viewing angle between the camera and acrylic plate so that ghost reflections focus completely outside the camera's field of view and depth of field. This realizes uniform, glare-free RGB illumination across the entire contact surface.
Additionally, the elastomer can be easily detached and replaced when worn out without replacing the base unit, maintaining consistent illumination conditions during prolonged grasping experiments.

### III-B Sensor Fabrication Procedure
Structural components and casting molds were 3D printed. After vacuum degassing and curing the transparent silicone, a custom coating mixture of silicone paint (Psycho Paint), white pigment, and thinner in a 0.3:1:1:2 ratio was airbrushed uniformly to form a thin, matte diffuse reflective layer.

### III-C Depth Reconstruction via Photometric Stereo
A high-precision calibration sphere with a diameter of 6 mm (radius $R=3\text{ mm}$) was pressed using a 3-axis stage to calculate theoretical surface gradients $[p_{ref}, q_{ref}]$ inside the contact region from its known geometry. A mapping function $f$ is then trained to predict surface gradients from pixel coordinates $(x,y)$ and RGB intensities $I(x,y)$.
When an unseen object is pressed, the acquired RGB image passes through $f$ to obtain a dense gradient field $[p(x,y), q(x,y)]$. Solving the Poisson equation (Poisson integration) accurately reconstructs the physical 3D depth map $z(x,y)$ of the contact region.

sections.heading: Large-Scale RGB-D Tactile Dataset and Dual-Head TimeSformer
sections.summary: Using 15 daily objects and tools, the authors built a multi-task RGB-D dataset consisting of 7,925 slip sequences (63,400 frames) and roughly 19,000 static images. For slip detection, a Dual-Head TimeSformer with Divided Space-Time Attention was adopted and trained using a masked joint loss that backpropagates direction loss only during slip.
sections.details:
Capitalizing on the hardware advantage where texture brightness changes are unobstructed by uneven lighting, the authors built a comprehensive dataset and designed a unified perception framework.

### IV-A & IV-B Tactile Dataset Construction
They selected 15 representative daily objects—including screwdrivers, scissors, keys, fruit, and USB connectors—encompassing hard, soft, smooth, and fine-textured surfaces.
- Static material and object classification subset: Approx. 19,336 high-resolution images captured across diverse contact poses, positions, and pressing depths.
- Dynamic slip subset: 7,925 sequences of 8 frames each (resized to $224\times 224$), totaling about 63,400 frames.
Contact state labels are categorized into three values: "Static," "Pressing," and "Slip." For "Slip," samples are further annotated into 8 directions in $45^{\circ}$ increments to directly assist grasp control. Every RGB sample is synchronously paired with a dense depth map generated via photometric stereo.

### IV-C Unified Perception Framework
1) Slip Detection Network (Dual-Head TimeSformer)
Input 8-frame tensors are patch-embedded and passed through Divided Space-Time Attention blocks that alternately compute Temporal Attention and Spatial Attention. This captures long-range spatiotemporal correlations while keeping computational costs manageable.
From the final layer's global token, two fully connected heads branch out:
- State Head: Classifies the three contact states (Static / Press / Slip).
- Direction Head: Predicts the 8 slip directions.
During training, the following masked joint loss function is used:
$$\mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{state} + \lambda \cdot \mathbb{I}_{\{state=Slip\}} \mathcal{L}_{dir}$$
Here, $\mathbb{I}$ is an indicator function that equals 1 only when the ground truth state is "Slip." This avoids computing direction loss on static or pressing data, preventing unnecessary gradient noise from corrupting the direction head.

2) Static Material Classification (ResNet-50)
To distinguish the 15 object categories from a single static tactile frame, a ResNet-50 pre-trained on ImageNet was used. Thanks to uniform illumination, the model avoids false highlights and reliably classifies objects based on pure surface microstructures, such as pores and edges.

sections.heading: Over 90% Slip Direction Accuracy on Unseen Objects and 72 µm Depth Precision
sections.summary: Depth reconstruction achieved a high precision with a plane-aligned RMSE of 0.072 mm. In dynamic slip tests on five unseen objects, the model reached 95.5% state accuracy and 91.5% 8-directional slip accuracy, alongside an outstanding 98.8% accuracy on 15-class static object recognition.
sections.details:
Experiments were carried out with the sensor mounted on a RealMan RM75-6F manipulator and a DH-Robotics AG-160-95 gripper. Training and inference were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU.

### V-B Evaluation of 3D Depth Reconstruction
Evaluating depth reconstruction with the reference sphere yielded a plane-aligned root mean square error (RMSE) of only 0.072 mm (approx. 72 µm). Removing mechanical mounting tilts confirmed sub-millimeter geometric recovery, verifying that reflection suppression under uniform illumination functioned effectively.

### V-C Evaluation of Dynamic Slip Detection
Across the full test set using RGB sequences, accuracy reached 99.69% for 3-state classification and 98.86% for 8-direction classification. When using reconstructed depth videos as inputs, accuracies were 94.51% and 70.57%, respectively. This shows that tracking fine displacements benefits significantly more from high-frequency texture in raw RGB images than from geometric depth information that has been smoothed out during reconstruction.

To test the crucial "generalization to unseen objects," an evaluation was run on 1,200 sequences (400 per state) across 5 objects excluded from training:
- Contact state classification (Static / Press / Slip): 95.5% accuracy.
- Slip direction classification (8 directions): 91.5% accuracy on samples identified as slip.
Confusion matrix analysis showed that directional misclassifications were predominantly concentrated in "adjacent 45-degree angles," demonstrating physically consistent, low-catastrophe predictions.

### V-D Evaluation of Static Tactile Object Classification
In 15-class object recognition on roughly 4,600 test images, the model achieved an impressive 98.8% accuracy with RGB inputs and 96.06% with depth map inputs. Grad-CAM visual attention maps confirmed that the model focused on sharp contours and characteristic microscopic patterns rather than lighting inconsistencies.

captions.F8: The 3D depth reconstruction pipeline. A contact mask is extracted from the RGB image, surface gradients in X/Y directions are predicted with the trained model, and masked Poisson integration yields a depth map with an RMSE of 0.072 mm.

sections.heading: Summary and Prospects for Integration into Multi-Fingered Hands
sections.summary: Combining a glare-free uniform RGB illumination sensor with a Dual-Head TimeSformer enables high-precision depth reconstruction and accurate slip direction detection on unseen objects. Future work aims to integrate this sensor into multi-fingered hands for real-time adaptive grasping combining vision, touch, and proprioception.
sections.details:
This paper presented a markerless visuo-tactile sensor that optical engineering frees from reflection artifacts, alongside a spatiotemporal deep learning framework.
- The sensor independently achieves sub-millimeter 3D shape reconstruction with a precision of 72 µm.
- By establishing a multi-task RGB-D dataset of 15 objects and applying spatiotemporal processing via TimeSformer, the authors demonstrated 95.5% contact state accuracy and 91.5% slip direction accuracy on unseen objects.
- It also achieved 98.8% accuracy in static object recognition, showing high-fidelity tactile sensing across both shape and texture.

For future work, the authors plan to embed this sensor into the fingertips of multi-fingered dexterous robot hands. By fusing high-frequency tactile feedback with global vision from external cameras and joint torque proprioception in real time, they aim to realize dynamic, closed-loop manipulation where fingers coordinate to regrasp the instant an unfamiliar object begins to slip.

takeaways: Even with a markerless visuo-tactile sensor, eliminating glare through uniform lighting and diffusers enables high-precision 8-directional slip detection purely by tracking fine texture displacement.
For slip direction estimation, utilizing high-frequency texture changes directly from raw RGB images is vastly superior in accuracy (91.5% vs. 70.57%) compared to using depth maps.
Divided Space-Time Attention in the TimeSformer video model serves as an ideal backbone for capturing subtle spatiotemporal displacements in tactile sequences.
limitations: Slip direction classification is restricted to a discrete 8-class representation (45-degree intervals), without direct regression of continuous slip velocity or rotational components (torsional slip).

Experiments are limited to gripper grasping evaluations and offline inference; closed-loop control feeding slip results back to robot arm force control loops in real-time (millisecond order) has not been demonstrated.
Quantitative verification is lacking regarding the long-term durability of the airbrushed white coating on the silicone rubber against peeling under heavy frictional contact.
